Revelations in Which He Might Glory: But He Rather Glories in Infirmities, as Calling Forth Christ's Power: Signs of His Apostleship: His Disinterestedness: Not That He Is Excusing Himself to Them; but He Does All for Their Good, lest He Should Find Them Not Such as He Desired, and So Should Have to Be Severe at His Coming.<div eID="gen34740" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34741" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17389"/>1. He proceeds to illustrate the "glorying in infirmities" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.11.30">2Co 11:30</reference>). He gave one instance which might expose him to ridicule (<reference osisRef="2Cor.11.33">2Co 11:33</reference>); he now gives another, but this one connected with a glorious revelation of which it was the sequel: but he dwells not on the glory done to himself, but on the infirmity which followed it, as displaying Christ's power. The oldest manuscripts read, "I MUST NEEDS boast (or glory) though it be not expedient; for I will come." The "for" gives a proof that it is "not expedient to boast": I will take the case of revelations, in which if anywhere boasting might be thought harmless. "Visions" refers to things seen: "revelations," to things heard (compare <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.15">1Sa 9:15</reference>) or revealed in any way. In "visions" their signification was not always vouchsafed; in "revelations" there was always an unveiling of truths before hidden (<reference osisRef="Dan.2.19">Da 2:19</reference>, 31). All parts of Scripture alike are matter of inspiration; but not all of revelation. There are degrees of revelation; but not of inspiration.<div eID="gen34741" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34742" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of--</hi>that is, from the Lord; Christ, <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.2">2Co 12:2</reference>. <div eID="gen34742" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17390"/><div sID="gen34743" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17390"/>2. Translate, "I know," not "I knew."<div eID="gen34743" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34744" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a man--</hi>meaning himself. But he purposely thus distinguishes between the rapt and glorified person of <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.2">2Co 12:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.4">4</reference>, and himself the infirmity-laden victim of the "thorn in the flesh" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.12.7">2Co 12:7</reference>). Such glory belonged not to him, but the weakness did. Nay, he did not even know whether he was in or out of the body when the glory was put upon him, so far was the glory from being his [Alford]. His spiritual self was his highest and truest self: the flesh with its infirmity merely his temporary self (<reference osisRef="Rom.7.25">Ro 7:25</reference>). Here, however, the latter is the prominent thought.<div eID="gen34744" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34745" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in Christ--</hi>a Christian (<reference osisRef="Rom.16.7">Ro 16:7</reference>).<div eID="gen34745" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34746" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">above--</hi>rather, simply "fourteen years ago." This Epistle was written A.D. 55-57. Fourteen years before will bring the vision to A.D. 41-43, the time of his second visit to Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Acts.22.17">Ac 22:17</reference>). He had long been intimate with the Corinthians, yet had never mentioned this revelation before: it was not a matter lightly to be spoken of.<div eID="gen34746" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34747" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I cannot tell--</hi>rather as Greek, "I know not." If in the body, he must have been caught up bodily; if out of the body, as seems to be Paul's opinion, his spirit must have been caught up out of the body. At all events he recognizes the possibility of conscious receptivity in disembodied spirits.<div eID="gen34747" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34748" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">caught up--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Acts.8.39">Ac 8:39</reference>).<div eID="gen34748" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34749" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to the third heaven--</hi>even to, &c. These raptures (note the plural, "visions," "revelations," <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.1">2Co 12:1</reference>) had two degrees: first he was caught up "to the third heaven," and from thence to "Paradise" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.12.4">2Co 12:4</reference>) [Clement of Alexandria, Miscellanies, 5.427], which seems to denote an inner recess of the third heaven [Bengel] (<reference osisRef="Luke.23.43">Lu 23:43</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.2.7">Re 2:7</reference>). Paul was permitted not only to "hear" the things of Paradise, but to see also in some degree the things of the third heaven (compare "visions," <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.1">2Co 12:1</reference>). The occurrence TWICE of "whether in the body ... I know not, God knoweth," and of "lest I should be exalted above measure," marks two stages in the revelation. "Ignorance of the mode does not set aside the certain knowledge of the fact. The apostles were ignorant of many things" [Bengel]. The first heaven is that of the clouds, the air; the second, that of the stars, the sky; the third is spiritual (<reference osisRef="Eph.4.10">Ep 4:10</reference>). <div eID="gen34749" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17392"/><div sID="gen34752" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17392"/><hi type="bold">4. unspeakable--</hi>not in themselves, otherwise Paul could not have heard them; but as the explanation states, "which it is not lawful ... to utter" [Alford]. They were designed for Paul's own consolation, and not for communication to others. Some heavenly words are communicable (<reference osisRef="Exod.34.6">Ex 34:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.6.3">Is 6:3</reference>). These were not so. Paul had not the power adequately to utter; nor if he had, would he have been permitted; nor would earthly men comprehend them (<reference osisRef="John.3.12">Joh 3:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.9">1Co 2:9</reference>). A man may hear and know more than he can speak. <div eID="gen34752" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17393"/><div sID="gen34753" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17393"/><hi type="bold">5. of myself--</hi>concerning myself. Self is put in the background, except in respect to his infirmities. His glorying in his other self, to which the revelations were vouchsafed, was not in order to give glory to his fleshly self, but to bring out in contrast the "infirmities" of the latter, that Christ might have all the glory. <div eID="gen34753" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17394"/><div sID="gen34754" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17394"/><hi type="bold">6. For--</hi>Not but that I might glory as to "myself" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.12.5">2Co 12:5</reference>); "FOR if I should desire to glory, I shall not be a fool"; for I have things to glory, or boast of which are good matter for glorying of (not mere external fleshly advantages which when he gloried in [2Co 11:1-33] he termed such glorying "folly," <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.1">2Co 11:1</reference>, 16, 17).<div eID="gen34754" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34755" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">think of me--</hi>Greek, "form his estimate respecting me."<div eID="gen34755" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34756" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">heareth of me--</hi>Greek, "heareth aught from me." Whatever haply he heareth from me in person. If on account of healing a cripple (<reference osisRef="Acts.14.12">Ac 14:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.14.13">13</reference>), and shaking off a viper (<reference osisRef="Acts.28.5">Ac 28:5</reference>), the people thought him a god, what would they have not done, if he had disclosed those revelations? [Estius]. I wish each of you to estimate me by "what he sees" my present acts and "hears" my teaching to be; not by my boasting of past revelations. They who allow themselves to be thought of more highly than is lawful, defraud themselves of the honor which is at God's disposal [Bengel] (<reference osisRef="John.5.44">Joh 5:44</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.12.43">12:43</reference>). <div eID="gen34756" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17395"/><div sID="gen34757" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17395"/><hi type="bold">7. exalted above measure--</hi>Greek, "overmuch uplifted." How dangerous must self-exaltation be, when even the apostle required so much restraint! [Bengel].<div eID="gen34757" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34758" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">abundance--</hi>Greek, "the excess"; exceeding greatness.<div eID="gen34758" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34759" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">given ... me--</hi>namely, by God (<reference osisRef="Job.5.6">Job 5:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.1.29">Php 1:29</reference>).<div eID="gen34759" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34760" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thorn in the flesh--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Num.33.55">Nu 33:55</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.28.24">Eze 28:24</reference>). Alford thinks it to be the same bodily affliction as in <reference osisRef="Gal.4.13">Ga 4:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gal.4.14">14</reference>. It certainly was something personal, affecting him individually, and not as an apostle: causing at once acute pain (as "thorn" implies) and shame ("buffet": as slaves are buffeted, <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.20">1Pe 2:20</reference>).<div eID="gen34760" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34761" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">messenger of Satan--</hi>who is permitted by God to afflict His saints, as Job (<reference osisRef="Job.2.7">Job 2:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.13.16">Lu 13:16</reference>).<div eID="gen34761" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34762" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to buffet me--</hi>In Greek, present: to buffet me even now continuously. After experiencing the state of the blissful angels, he is now exposed to the influence of an evil angel. The chastisement from hell follows soon upon the revelation from heaven. As his sight and hearing had been ravished with heavenly "revelations," so his touch is pained with the "thorn in the flesh." <div eID="gen34762" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17400"/><div sID="gen34782" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17400"/><hi type="bold">12. Truly, &c.--</hi>There is understood some such clause as this, "And yet I have not been commended by you."<div eID="gen34782" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34783" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in all patience, in signs, &c.--</hi>The oldest manuscripts omit "in." "Patience" is not one of the "signs," but the element IN which they were wrought: endurance of opposition which did not cause me to leave off working [Alford]. Translate, "In ... patience, BY signs," &c. His mode of expression is modest, putting himself, the worker, in the background, "were wrought," not "I wrought." As the signs have not been transmitted to us, neither has the apostleship. The apostles have no literal successors (compare <reference osisRef="Acts.1.21">Ac 1:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.22">22</reference>).<div eID="gen34783" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34784" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">mighty deeds--</hi>palpable works of divine omnipotence. The silence of the apostles in fourteen Epistles, as to miracles, arises from the design of those Epistles being hortatory, not controversial. The passing allusions to miracles in seven Epistles prove that the writers were not enthusiasts to whom miracles seem the most important thing. Doctrines were with them the important matter, save when convincing adversaries. In the seven Epistles the mention of miracles is not obtrusive, but marked by a calm air of assurance, as of facts acknowledged on all hands, and therefore unnecessary to dwell on. This is a much stronger proof of their reality than if they were formally and obtrusively asserted. Signs and wonders is the regular formula of the Old Testament, which New Testament readers would necessarily understand of supernatural works. Again, in the Gospels the miracles are so inseparably and congruously tied up with the history, that you cannot deny the former without denying the latter also. And then you have a greater difficulty than ever, namely, to account for the rise of Christianity; so that the infidel has something infinitely more difficult to believe than that which he rejects, and which the Christian more rationally accepts. <div eID="gen34784" type="x-p"/>

entries.reader_content_plain: 18. I desired Titus-- namely, to go unto you. Not the mission mentioned 2Co 8:6 , 17, 22; but a mission previous to this Epistle, probably that from which he had just returned announcing to Paul their penitence ( 2Co 7:6-16 ). a brother-- rather "OUR (literally, 'the') brother"; one well known to the Corinthians, and perhaps a Corinthian; probably one of the two mentioned in 2Co 8:18 , 22 . same spirit-- inwardly. steps-- outwardly.

entries.content_plain: 21. my God-- his God, however trying the humiliation that was in store for him. will humble me-- The indicative implies that the supposition will actually be so. The faithful pastor is "humbled" at, and "bewails" the falls of his people, as though they were his own. sinned already-- before my last coming [Bengel], that is, before the second visit which he paid, and in which he had much at Corinth to rebuke. have not repented-- shall not have repented [Alford]. uncleanness-- for example, of married persons ( 1Th 4:7 ). fornication-- among the unmarried.
